opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think rapid iteration has really changed how I approach research, almost at a philosophical level.

When I was trained in physics, the culture was to think very carefully before you do anything: derive things on paper, build a clean theory, and only then check it against experiments. In machine learning, especially now, the cost of running an experiment is often much lower than the cost of thinking very hard about it. So the loop becomes: have a rough idea, write a small piece of code, run it in an afternoon, look at what happens, and let the result tell you whether the idea is worth pursuing.

What I've learned is that this changes not just the speed, but the direction. A lot of my more interesting projects didn't start from a grand plan. They started from a toy experiment where something unexpected happened, like a curve that looked strange or a network that learned a structure I didn't anticipate. If I'd been iterating slowly, I probably would have dismissed that as noise. Because I could rerun it ten times with small variations, I could tell it was real and then follow it.

I also try to keep my setups as small and interpretable as possible, almost like a physicist's toy model. Small models let you iterate in minutes rather than weeks, and they let you actually look inside and understand what's going on. I think there's a real tension in the field right now: scaling gives you capability, but small, fast experiments give you understanding. I tend to bet on understanding, partly because that's where I feel I have a comparative advantage as an individual researcher rather than a big lab.

There's a caveat, though. Rapid iteration can turn into a kind of random walk if you're not careful. You run lots of experiments, get lots of results, and none of them add up to anything. So I try to balance it: fast loops at the bottom, but at the top some slower, more stubborn questions I keep coming back to. For me, those are things like "Can we make neural networks more interpretable?" and "Can AI help us do science, and can science help us understand AI?" The quick experiments are how I explore, but those bigger questions are what keep the exploration pointed somewhere.

So I'd say rapid iteration makes the research more empirical and more surprise-driven, but you still need taste and a few long-term convictions to turn those surprises into something meaningful.

r001.rationale: The candidate says rapid iteration changes not just research speed but its direction, describing how repeated quick experiments and unexpected results lead them to pursue new lines of work.

fable-5.1.text:
Rapid iteration has really shaped how I do research, maybe more than any single idea has. When I started my PhD, I thought research was about having a brilliant idea, carefully working it out, and then presenting it to the world. What I found instead is that most of my good ideas came out of a loop: try something small, look at what happens, be surprised, adjust, try again. The KAN work is a good example. The first version was honestly a bit of a toy. We had a hunch that learnable activation functions on edges could be interesting, we coded it up in a few days, and the early results were not amazing. But because the iteration was cheap, we could keep poking at it. Add sparsification here, try grid extension there, visualize the splines and see if they match the function we expected. Each small experiment taught us something, and the direction of the project emerged from that process rather than from a grand plan.

I think this matters especially for the kind of work I care about, which sits between physics and machine learning. Physicists have a tradition of toy models. You strip a problem down to the simplest thing that still captures the phenomenon, you play with it, and you build intuition before going big. Machine learning today makes that very natural. You can run a tiny network on a synthetic dataset in minutes, and that tiny network often tells you more about the mechanism than a giant model would, because you can actually see everything that is going on. So rapid iteration for me is not just about speed. It is a way of thinking. It keeps me honest, because my intuitions are wrong a lot more often than I would like to admit, and the fastest way to find that out is to run the experiment.

The flip side is that there is a danger of getting trapped in local optima. If you only ever do what is fast, you tend to do what is easy, and sometimes the important questions require slowing down, reading an old paper from the 1950s, or sitting with a piece of math for a few weeks. So I try to balance it. Fast loops for exploration, slow thinking for choosing which loops are worth running. The iteration tells you what is true. The slow part tells you what is interesting.

r001.rationale: The response says the project’s direction emerged through repeated small experiments and adjustments, clearly communicating that rapid iteration can continually reshape research direction.

astra-6.text:
I think rapid iteration changes not just how quickly you do research, but which questions you decide to pursue. You start with an intuition, try a small experiment, and the result often reveals that the interesting question is slightly different from the one you started with. So the direction emerges through that back-and-forth between ideas and evidence.

But I think you also need time to step back. If you only focus on experiments that give you quick feedback, you can miss questions that require sustained effort. For me, the value of rapid iteration is that it lets you test assumptions early, so you can make a more informed decision about where to go deeper.

r001.rationale: The response says experiments can reveal a different interesting question and that research direction emerges through the back-and-forth between ideas and evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think rapid iteration helps me discover what the research question really is. You start with an intuition, try a small experiment, and often the result surprises you. Then you revise your understanding and try again. That feedback loop can move the research in a direction you wouldn’t have anticipated at the beginning.

But I also think you need time to step back. If you only focus on running the next experiment, you can end up optimizing something without asking whether it matters. So I try to move quickly when testing ideas, while being more deliberate about what the results mean and which questions are worth pursuing.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes repeated experiments and revisions as a feedback loop that can move research in an unexpected direction.
